text: Now, we are going to introduce you to GraphX, which we'll primarily cover as a hands-on presentation.
GraphX was developed by the Amplab at UC Berkeley and has now become an Apache product.
In this brief introduction, we are using a few slides from Amplab presentations.
Like Neo4j, GraphX uses a property graph model.
That means both nodes and edges can have attributes and values.
In GraphX, the node properties are stored in a vertex table,
and edge properties are stored in an edge table.
The connectivity information, that is, which edge connects to which nodes,
is stored separately from the node and edge properties.
Since GraphX is based on Spark, whose central information representation
is based on Resilient Distributed Datasets, or RDDs,
you may recall that RDDs are typically in-memory information objects.
These objects can be used to perform an action, which returns a value,
or they can perform a transformation, which can produce another RDD.
GraphX is built on special RDDs for vertices and edges.
Note that vertex IDs are defined to be unique by design.
Vertex RDD A represents a set of vertices, all of which have an attribute called A.
The Edge class is an object with a source vertex, a destination vertex, and an edge attribute.
The Edge RDD extends this basic edge by storing edges in a columnar format on each partition for performance.

that has both node properties and edge properties.
